name: Sara Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so tell me both what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Sara, 27, a lead developer at a tech company, and I have a master's in software. I check the morning error log, pair with another developer on tricky fixes, and get our weekly release ready; I like finding the small mistake that explains a whole messy customer problem. I use an AI assistant every day for test ideas, but late release calls can eat the evening I meant to spend with my partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our team the quiet outcome is useful: keep the tools that save an hour and stop selling them as magic. I already ask an assistant to draft test cases, then check each one against the ticket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my role is steady if the change stays small. I earn a normal lead salary, have about four months of expenses saved, and can see a few other software employers within reach; I don't need to make a dramatic move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the weekly release and write down where the test assistant gets things wrong. In the first year, I'd put the time saved into the customer login bug we keep postponing, and add a small amount to savings each pay day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. The login bug is annoying, but I can fix it without betting my rent on a prediction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the assistant get wrong recently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The assistant once suggested a test that passed even when the account was locked. I wrote a better one by hand, and now I use that case to check any new version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you save without changing your life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I transfer 100 into savings on pay day when there is room after bills. If a month is tight, I don't call that a failed plan; I skip that transfer.

say: I'd keep the **test assistant** for small tasks that survive review.
I'd tell colleagues to stop calling minor time savings **magic**.
think: I feel secure with **four months saved** and a few nearby software firms.
I see little reason to leave a **lead role** if this change stays small.
do: Keep leading the **weekly release** and checking generated test cases.
Fix the **customer login bug** using time freed by the assistant.
Transfer **100 on pay day** into savings when bills allow.
feel: **Calm** about the job and interested in clearing neglected work.
S0.quote: The login bug is annoying, but I can fix it without betting my rent on a prediction.
fieldNote: **Four months saved** and nearby employers make the mild scenario genuinely manageable for her.
She uses AI daily but remembers a **false passing test** and keeps a human check in the release process.

steps.text: Lead weekly software releases and check assistant-generated test cases
Transfer 100 to savings on pay days when bills allow

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should measure the tools against real faults, not just lines of code produced. Writing, checking and answering customers are much of our work, so fewer developers may be hired even if the company keeps shipping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be on a smaller team and might be expected to manage more releases with fewer people. My skill and savings give me room to experiment, but I would be kidding myself if I said a lead title made my income certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd run a six-week comparison of assistant-written fixes and human fixes on closed tickets, including mistakes and review time. In the first year of the shift, I'd learn how to audit AI-generated code, ask to own that review process, and hold back from signing a new flat lease until I see the staffing plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert and uneasy. The tools could make my job more interesting, and that interests me. A good trial can also tell the firm it needs fewer of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Whose work might disappear first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My teammate Joel handles the customer messages I tend to rush. If his post is not replaced, I could catch code errors and still miss why a client is angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the trial honest enough to trust?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell management the trial needs a count of time spent fixing bad output, not just time saved writing code. If that count is hidden, I wouldn't put my name on the report.

say: I'd ask for **fault counts** and review time alongside speed claims.
I'd say fewer **new hires** could follow even while software keeps shipping.
think: I may carry **more releases** with fewer colleagues.
My savings and skill give me room, but I cannot assume my **lead pay** is safe.
do: Run a **six-week comparison** using closed tickets and error counts.
Learn to **audit generated code** and seek ownership of that review.
Delay a **new flat lease** until the staffing plan is clear.
feel: **Uneasy** about staffing, with real interest in the new review work.
S1.quote: A good trial can also tell the firm it needs fewer of us.
fieldNote: **Writing and checking** are central to her job, so steady change threatens staffing despite strong skills.
Her open attitude includes an **honest error count** and a pause on housing commitments while pay is uncertain.

steps.text: Compare assistant and human fixes on closed tickets for six weeks
Study how to audit generated code and seek review ownership
Delay signing a new flat lease until staffing plans are clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2028 reaches our screens immediately; robots arriving around 2031 don't buy developers three more years. The firm should tell people which paid tasks remain before it cuts posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might lose the lead job or take a much lower wage, and four months of savings could vanish during a long search. I use AI every day, but that doesn't make me immune to a cheaper system that can design and verify software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd map my spending and put another 50 into savings on pay day if our bills allow, working toward six months of expenses without pretending I already have it. I'd ask two nearby firms about paid security roles, and if my post is cut in the first year after 2028, I'd apply for those roles; if none exist, I'd take a short contract only if it covers rent while I search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, though I have a list rather than a blank page. I would tell my partner I am delaying any larger flat until we know the income survives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner that evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We share a small flat, and my partner teaches music part time; that income won't cover both our bills. I'd show them the rent and savings numbers rather than promise everything is fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What support would you ask of your employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the firm for at least a paid handover or funded training if it removes my role. I can do the learning, but I can't ask my partner to finance the entire landing.

say: I'd say **2028 thinking AI** reaches code before robots arrive around 2031.
I'd demand a list of **paid remaining tasks** before cuts.
think: I could lose **lead pay** despite using AI every day.
My **four-month cushion** might run out before another suitable job appears.
do: Map **household spending** and save another 50 on pay day if bills allow.
Ask **two nearby firms** about paid security openings now.
Apply after a cut, accepting a **short contract** only if it covers rent.
feel: **Alarmed** about household income, even with a plan.
S2.quote: I use AI every day, but that doesn't make me immune to a cheaper system that can design and verify software.
fieldNote: **High exposure** hits her code and verification work in 2028; later robots provide no delay.
Her partner's **part-time music pay** cannot carry the household, so she checks actual vacancies and contract wages.

steps.text: Map household bills and save another 50 on pay day if affordable
Apply for paid security roles at two nearby firms after a cut
Delay a larger shared flat until income is secure
Take short contract after cut only if no security role exists and rent covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years before 2031 lets us see which AI reviews are useful and which ones just look neat. The robots come around 2034, but our desk work changes with the thinking system first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could build a genuine audit role if clients still pay for accountable human review. I don't know that they will, so I'd keep a savings target and look at employers outside my current firm while the market still has choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager for a paid rotation into security review next spring and take the certified security course only if both the rotation is agreed and the firm funds the course. If that rotation never appears, I'd use one evening a week on free practice labs instead; in the first year after 2031, I'd apply for paid audit roles and leave only for an offer that covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than frozen. Five years is long enough to test a path, but I would still look at every rent renewal carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a paid rotation have to include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A paid rotation means my salary continues while I learn; a course alone does not give that. I'd want the manager to put the hours and duties in writing before paying for an exam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the two of you change housing plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would keep teaching if bookings hold, and we'd keep the same flat for now. I wouldn't plan a bigger place around an income we have not actually earned.

say: I'd say **2031 thinking AI** reaches coding before 2034 robots.
I'd ask for **paid review work** rather than a vague promise of new roles.
think: I might build an **audit role** if clients pay for human accountability.
I need **actual offers** and savings before trusting that plan.
do: Ask for a **paid security rotation** next spring.
Take the **security course** only if rotation and funding are agreed; otherwise use free practice labs weekly.
Apply for **paid audit roles** after 2031 and leave only for an offer covering our bills.
feel: **Uneasy**, but able to test a path over five years.
S3.quote: A paid rotation means my salary continues while I learn; a course alone does not give that.
fieldNote: **Five years** let her seek paid learning while keeping normal salary, rather than buying a credential on faith.
She keeps the shared **flat unchanged** and ties any later job switch to actual paid offers.

steps.text: Request a paid security review rotation next spring
Take security course only with paid rotation and funding; otherwise use free labs weekly
Apply for paid audit roles after 2031; leave only for bill-covering offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade allows people to build a second skill without abandoning the work they like. Coding still faces thinking AI in 2036; the robots around 2039 are a later issue for physical work, not a cushion for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 37 I might have several years of security review and enough savings to choose my hours. I might also be doing the same code work for less money; the ten years only help if I take steps and the paid work exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep a record of the faults I caught and add to my emergency fund each month while the job lasts. I'd take a funded security qualification if offered, and in the first year after 2036 I'd compare paid security, release review and contract work, moving roles only for a better signed offer. My partner and I would discuss a larger flat only after the pay is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm about the next few years, though not smug. I have time to build options and a cushion, and I'd still check the rent each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would go into that record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The record would include the broken lockout test, the customer login fix and what I changed. If a future employer asks what I actually did, I can show outcomes instead of saying I was 'AI ready'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a bigger flat sensible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner that we can make the bigger-flat decision together once there is a signed offer. A ten-year prediction isn't a salary slip.

say: I'd say **2036 thinking AI** affects code before 2039 robots.
I'd advise developers to keep **proof of solved faults**.
think: I could have **years of review work** by 37 if paying clients want it.
I might still face **lower code pay**, even with time to prepare.
do: Keep a **fault record** and add to emergency savings monthly.
Take a **funded security qualification** if the firm offers one.
Compare **paid roles** after 2036 and move only for a better signed offer.
feel: **Calm for now**, with attention to yearly rent and future demand.
S4.quote: A ten-year prediction isn't a salary slip.
fieldNote: **Four months saved** and some local options support calm about the next few years, despite uncertain later pay.
Her plan rests on **documented work**, funded study and signed offers before any housing change.

steps.text: Record solved software faults and outcomes while employed
Add money to emergency savings each month while wages last
Take a security qualification if employer funds it
Move to security or release review after 2036 only for better signed offer

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because even a good lead could lose pay quickly. A clear list of paid roles, time for a handover, and funded security training before any cut would help me make a sensible move.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I enjoy the tools. I do, often; I want the time AI tools save to become better software and decent work, not a quiet reason to drop people.

headlineQuote: I want the time AI tools save to become better software and decent work, not a quiet reason to drop people.
portrait: Sara is a **27-year-old lead developer** with a master's degree who uses AI daily and checks its test ideas.
Her **typical pay**, four-month cushion and some nearby jobs give her room to experiment, while her partner teaches music part time.
She stays **calm** under AI Plateau but worries steady disruption could leave fewer developers carrying more releases.
Fast 2028 AGI **alarms** her because code and verification could cheapen before household bills change.
With more time, she seeks **funded security work**, records solved faults and compares real wages before moving flats.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut her lead pay while her partner's part-time music income cannot cover both their bills.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid role clarity**, handover time and funded security training before cuts would support a job move.
